system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 30 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.

PRMT6 loss perturbs arginine methylation and translational/transcriptional control; resulting proteostatic or amino-acid imbalance may increase reliance on GCN2-mediated integrated stress response.

CDKN2A-deleted cells have unrestrained CDK4/6 activity and proliferative/mitotic stress; UNC45A (HSP90 co-chaperone for myosin, mitotic spindle/proliferation roles) may become more limiting. Modest but pan-lineage effect.

input.summary: I searched for selective dependencies created by tumor-suppressor loss or other loss-of-function alterations, leaving out paralog pairs. None of the five hypotheses I registered and tested replicated. Notes on the survey: (1) Most of the strongest LOSS/MUT hits genome-wide were markers of a disease subtype rather than of the alteration itself. Many were blood-cancer subtype markers, e.g. MPL, MEF2C, FLT3, POU2AF1, CSK and LRP8 hits in lymphoid/myeloid lines. Others likely reflected lineage or mutation burden: the MYH14, JUP and POU2AF3 hits that recur across many MUT biomarkers, and CIC→TRADD, which was driven by lymphoid lines. (2) Classic tumor suppressors gave weak signals after lineage adjustment, with no FDR-significant non-essential hits. Tested: KEAP1, ARID1A, PTEN, STK11, NF1, NF2, FBXW7, RB1, SMARCA4, SMAD4, BAP1, PBRM1, KMT2D, EP300, APC and RNF43 mutations, plus LOSS_CDKN2A and LOSS_MTAP. (3) I registered five candidates with no prior literature found. Each held across lineages in discovery, but all failed in both held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens, so they were most likely false positives from small altered groups (n=11–22) and the very large number of tests. One choice was weak in hindsight: CDKN2A→UNC45A rested on a large group but a tiny effect. The honest conclusion is that this dataset gave no reproducible, non-paralog loss-of-function dependency from my candidates. The discovery-only signals should be treated as noise.

findings.claim: Lines with damaging STAG2 mutations did not depend more on GCN2 (EIF2AK4) in held-out data (Broad p=0.60; Sanger p=0.88), despite a discovery signal across lineages (t=-4.3).
ST6GALNAC4 expression loss predicted UGCG dependency in discovery (t=-6.7), but the effect reversed in held-out Broad lines (p=0.999) and was absent in Sanger (p=0.29).
SMAD4 loss did not confer increased HDAC4 dependency in held-out Broad (p=0.90) or Sanger (p=0.16) screens.
PRMT6 loss did not predict GCN2 dependency in held-out Broad (p=0.36) or Sanger (p=0.37) screens.
The small discovery association between CDKN2A loss and UNC45A dependency (beta about -0.11) did not replicate (Broad p=0.25; Sanger p=0.38).
